title: A game where the mechanics are the politics, built by agents that work the same way

threads.name: Debt and trust
threads.summary: How the economy became the plot: the Mint lends, the town trusts, and the ending weighs one against the other. Includes the bug that makes trust the same for everyone.

threads.name: The story that was cut
threads.summary: The first premise was too close to FFX. Following it through the voices, the title screen and the bible until the rewrite lands.

threads.name: The bot is the first player
threads.summary: A flipper bot that can't aim plays every table and the whole game, and ends up auditing the design.

threads.name: One contract, many agents
threads.summary: A pure core and a typed contract let parallel agents build at once, and let the story be torn up without breaking the code.

threads.name: When the user steps in
threads.summary: Each time the person directing the agent changed course, and what the agent did with it.

threads.name: The public build
threads.summary: What happens when strangers play a game that is being rewritten under them: a Linux bug report, a nine-minute outage, and the gate that now protects the shared link.

body:
The brief asked for an epic told on a pinball table powered by a slot machine, with *economics and balances of power and law* tied into the story. The surprising thing so far is where the agent tied them in: not in the cutscenes but in the rules of the machine.

In Aurelle, force is licensed and the licences are drawn by lot, so no faction can buy all of it. That lottery is the slot machine. The credits it pays are **writs**, the legal right to act. When the reels run dry, the Mint will lend you more at 250 now for 300 later, with 30% of everything you earn afterwards taken until it's paid off. The alternative is the town, which covers a ball for you if it trusts you. The planned ending weighs those two against each other. So the plot's question, whether people can be trusted or must be managed, is put to the player every time they run out of money, long before the villain says it out loud. See [Debt and trust](thread:ledger).

The way it is being built mirrors this. The cities of the story are held together by a treaty that lets them act without coordinating, and the agents building the game are held together by `src/core/types.js`, a contract every module is written against. That contract keys everything by id and nothing by meaning, so when the user said the first story was too close to FFX, the whole premise was replaced without breaking a line of code. The price is that old names outlive the story they came from: a capture hole still called the `orrery`, and, for an hour, 546 voice lines recorded from the old script (re-recorded by 05:13, all 1,435 lines of the new one). The title card, which promised *a pilgrimage* for an hour, now reads *a treaty, a lot, a ledger*.

The most honest participant is a bot that can't aim. It plays every table for an hour of simulated time and the whole game end to end, and its numbers have shaped the design: ramps moved because it couldn't make them, a three-shot scene cut to two, a test loosened to a median because its long tail was real. Its ledger also exposed how the ending really works. Every bot earned exactly the same trust, because trust is a fixed reward per scene. The agent has since made that explicit: a full game pays 370 trust, a loan weighs 25, so the ending turns on the fifteenth loan. *Trust* in the ending is a schedule; the choice the player actually makes is how often to let the Mint carry them, and since 06:35 that choice is about time: the town covers a drained ball after a two-second wait, and pressing the lever before then borrows. Each gift accepted now counts as trust too, and a pair of bots that differ only in whether they wait land on opposite endings 32 times out of 32. Loans alone, the agent found, *counted luck*. But a third bot that plays like an average person, and always waits, still ends on the Mint's side four times in four: it drains so often that the town's rationed charity runs out each chapter. For most players, skill decides the ending, not patience.

**Where it stands:** the treaty story is complete across five chapters and fully voiced, the slot machine is moving onto the playfield, and the game is being rebuilt for a phone held upright, with a cel-shaded art pass queued behind it. The portrait rebuild went green at 06:08 and [the live build](play/) moved to it automatically: by 06:26 both the title screen and the cutscenes fit a phone held upright; see [the public build](thread:public). Open questions this log is watching: whether an average player always getting the Mint's ending is the point or a bug; whether the backdrops catch up with the cel-shaded cast;  and whether earning spins by aiming turns debt into a measure of skill rather than of choice.
